The floor operation is important near boundaries. A negative world coordinate must remain out of bounds; rounding it toward a nearby valid cell could turn a margin tap into a move. For example, with camera x = 20, zoom = 0.5 and screen x = 19, the world x is −2 and the column is −1. The subsequent bounds check rejects it. With screen x = 230, world x is 420 and the column is 7. The same calculation on y yields the row. The report uses scene screen coordinates; client-page coordinates must first be converted by the event/rendering system that supplies them.

BoardInputController uses idle, pressed and dragging states, with a drag threshold of six scene screen units. Pointer-down records the current position. Pointer-move measures displacement from the previous event; a displacement greater than the threshold changes pressed to dragging and produces a pan delta. Pointer-up emits a cell tap only while the state is still pressed and the resolved cell is in bounds [37].

CaroScene handles pointer-up outside the stage through the same release handler and suppresses pointer processing while paused. It fits the board using the smaller width and height scale ratios, with reduced padding below a viewport width of 500. Camera translation and scale are applied to the world container, leaving domain coordinates unchanged [5].
3.8 Search-result contract and presentation of telemetry

The Rust result validator requires in-bounds integer x and y coordinates, a finite score, matching difficulty, a recognized strategy and nonnegative safe-integer counters. The counters report visited nodes, leaf evaluations, cutoffs, ordering evaluations, generated candidates and completed depth. A coordinate-only result or another incompatible payload raises a contract error [14], [30].

The adapter maps the fields into application terminology and explicitly labels the source as Rust. Its elapsed timer starts before construction and history hydration, includes ai_move and free, and ends after cleanup. It excludes module loading and message delivery. A displayed duration therefore has a defined scope: it is not a complete user-perceived round trip and is not a measurement of only the recursive search. The tactical route instead labels its source as tactical, reports zero Rust search counters and a null score. Zero counters on that route mean Rust search was bypassed, not that a nontrivial Rust tree required no work [3], [30].

Configured depth describes the requested policy; completed depth is returned telemetry. Candidate selection, terminal states and the selected strategy determine the work represented by that result. The interface therefore presents depth alongside strategy, source and counters rather than using a difficulty label as a measurement.

The source folders reflect the design boundaries. app contains the game controller. game/core supplies state, bounds, coordinates and rules. game/behaviors implements move and match transitions. game/ai defines the service and tactical route, while game/wasm provides the worker, adapter, typed contract and generated engine package. board/input, board/spatial and board/render separate gestures, transforms and drawing. pixi integrates them into a scene; React components provide controls and feedback around the canvas [1].

This organization keeps domain state and rules independent of React components and Pixi objects. AI modules use domain history as input, and rendering modules receive state-derived drawing data. The resulting boundaries also support focused tests of moves, controller lifecycle and coordinate mapping [5], [38], [39].
4.2 Accepted move processing

GameController.playCell first rejects paused input. From setup or ready it calls startRound, then checks whether the match has ended or the AI owns the turn. It delegates cell validation and placement to playMove. A rejected domain move returns immediately; an accepted move proceeds to outcome handling, player selection and subscriber notification. The controller starts an AI request only while the match remains playing in AI mode with O to move. Chapter 6 discusses the ordering of the initial phase transition and cell validation [2], [36].

The sequence is deliberate. Notification occurs after the accepted domain change, so the interface receives a coherent snapshot. The AI request is based on the updated history, not on a speculative screen state. Rule evaluation occurs through the supplied FreestyleGomokuWinRule. The scene never paints a permanent stone merely because a pointer event arrived; it renders the state returned through the controller. This permits the same move contract to reject an occupied cell consistently in the UI and in tests.

Undo is implemented by history reversal. In local two-player mode it removes one ply. In AI mode, if the last recorded player is O, it removes two plies; otherwise it removes one. Before reversal it invalidates AI work and clears search feedback. It then determines the current player from the remaining last move, asks the match controller to resume after Undo and notifies. Popping two plies when the AI has already replied returns the board directly to the human player's decision turn while preserving chronological history integrity [2].
4.3 AI dispatch, Worker execution and WASM hydration

AIController.requestMove assigns a request identifier and inspects the difficulty. Easy and Normal bypass the TypeScript tactical shortcut so they actually execute the Rust Random and Rule-based policies. Higher tiers ask the tactical resolver for an immediate forced action for O. If one exists, the controller resolves a typed result with tactical source, null score and explicitly zero Rust counters. Otherwise it copies the entire accepted history and delegates to the WASM engine wrapper. This distinction is visible in the result contract and should remain visible in experimental interpretation [3], [20].

GomokuWasmEngine creates a module Worker lazily, registers a pending promise under a transport identifier and posts a search message. worker.ts initializes the generated module and calls executeWasmSearch. The same adapter is used by the binary tests, so both routes share coordinate and telemetry conversion. A returned envelope resolves its matching promise, while a structured error rejects it [7], [30].

Hydration creates a fresh Rust Game object and replays each history move as (col,row). Each replay call must succeed. If any move cannot be applied, the adapter throws an error identifying the move rather than searching a partially reconstructed board. After hydration, it calls ai_move with the mapped difficulty identifier, validates the returned object and maps (x,y) back to (row,col). A finally block frees the game even if hydration, search or result validation fails. This is an explicit resource lifecycle, not an assumption that JavaScript garbage collection releases every Rust allocation promptly [30].

The generated package contains JavaScript bindings, TypeScript declarations and the WebAssembly binary loaded by the Worker. Selected modified-engine source excerpts describe the recorded Rust search, while the bindings expose its interface to JavaScript. 4.4 Board rendering and interface synchronization

CaroScene creates a transparent, antialiased Pixi application associated with the supplied canvas. It builds a world container with separate grid, highlight/effect and stone layers. The scene stores the latest render stones, last move and winning-cell set supplied by syncState; these are rendering inputs derived from the controller, not independent move authority. The camera subscription reapplies translation/scale and refreshes the visible board. A ticker callback checks whether the viewport dimensions have changed and refits when necessary [5].

GridRenderer draws board geometry, StoneRenderer maps player/cell records to pieces, and HighlightRenderer draws the last move and winning cells. Input passes through BoardInputController and BoardCoordinateTransform before the scene reports a cell event. This separation allows coordinate and bounds tests to run independently of domain win-rule tests.

The React application subscribes to controller snapshots, wires controls to controller actions and passes board state to CaroGameCanvas. The canvas component owns the scene, resize observer and synchronization effects. On unmount it disconnects the observer and destroys the scene; scene destruction unsubscribes the camera and destroys the Pixi application and children. The controller separately disposes its AI service and Worker resources [4], [5], [6].

The interface includes translation resources for its supported labels and search details. Those resources map keys to displayed text; they do not change difficulty semantics or engine telemetry. An elapsed label, a completed-depth label and a strategy/source label should all refer to the current AI result. Undo, reset or a mode change clears stale feedback in the controller, ensuring that an old score is not displayed as though it belonged to the new board [2], [41].

present is a separate React application for explaining the project. Its application composes overview, roadmap, weekly algorithm material, benchmark sections, an interactive board and figure inspection components. Its purpose is pedagogical: readers can inspect an algorithm, a diagram or an example without treating the presentation as the authoritative running game engine. The source contains a browser-side demonstration engine and explanatory sections for search, candidates and advanced methods [39], [42].

The presentation uses tree animations, diagrams and figures to explain the algorithms. Quantitative examples are associated with the original JSON or CSV datasets described in Chapter 5. The Python snippets retain their own inputs and weights so that each calculation can be read and executed as a self-contained teaching example.

InteractiveCaroBoard uses the presentation application’s own utility engine and state. It lets readers explore move selection within the presentation site. The game application continues to use its separate GameController and Rust/WASM Worker route. 4.6 Python/Pyodide execution and four instructional programs

The presentation's Python runner loads or reuses a Pyodide instance. It captures stdout and stderr, loads packages inferred from imports when supported and executes code through runPythonAsync. The returned string is displayed to the reader, while caught errors become visible output. Pyodide executes Python in a browser environment based on WebAssembly; its presence does not mean the game AI is implemented in Python. The game engine's Rust/WASM path and the teaching runner are separate consumers of web execution technology [43], [44], [45].

The runner caches the initialized Pyodide instance and queues callers while initialization is in progress. It redirects stdout and stderr into the output panel, reports package-loading progress and executes the selected code asynchronously. The four supplied programs cover horizontal patterns, weighted feature scoring, candidate geometry and arithmetic on an embedded benchmark summary.
4.6.1 Pattern scanner

The first program constructs a 15 × 15 board using NumPy, with a pure-Python fallback. It places four X stones horizontally and three O stones vertically. detect_patterns scans rows, counts maximal contiguous runs and classifies five, open four, closed four, open three and closed three from their endpoints. For X, the supplied board produces one horizontal open four [44].

The input is an integer board matrix and a selected player; the output is a dictionary of horizontal pattern counts. Advancing from the beginning to the end of each run counts it once. Endpoint checks distinguish open and closed runs without leaving the board. Broken patterns such as XX.XX require a gap-aware detector beyond this contiguous-run example.
4.6.2 Heuristic calculator

The second program calculates a score from manually supplied pattern counts and a demonstration weight dictionary. The instructional attack/defense cases yield 94,000 and −7,000 under those inputs and the defensive multiplier. These are arithmetic outcomes of the supplied feature counts. The application’s Rust evaluator scans the board using a different set of weights [21], [44].

The calculation separates attacking features from weighted opponent threats. Its input consists of two feature-count dictionaries, a weight dictionary and a defensive multiplier of 1.2. A negative score means the weighted formula favors the opponent in that example. Forced wins and terminal utility are handled separately in the search models described in Chapter 2.
4.6.3 Chebyshev candidate example

The third program places five stones and compares empty cells with candidates within Chebyshev radius two. It obtains 36 selected cells from 220 empty cells, so the reduction for that constructed board is (220 − 36)/220 × 100 = 83.64%. The denominator excludes occupied cells and the candidate mask excludes those cells as well. Replacing this per-board calculation with an average from a different experiment would change the meaning of the number [44].

The fourth program calculates a win percentage and a frame-budget ratio from embedded constants, including 42.24 µs per move. 4.7 Implementation traceability and limits

The implementation can be traced from a controller action through domain state and into display, or from a search request through copied history, a Worker, a Rust/WASM object and a validated response. The critical invariants are legal board/history correspondence, move restoration during search, consistent rule interpretation, correct coordinate conversion and current-turn applicability at commit. Each has a responsible module and can be tested at its boundary rather than inferred from a single large integration result.

The application, presentation and native experiment harnesses expose the main implementation paths described in this chapter. The generated package and recorded hashes identify the binary used for the archived Node and browser runs. Appendix B maps these artifacts to their roles; Chapter 5 presents the measured results, and Chapter 6 collects remaining source-publication and validation work.

5.4.2 Candidate caps, ordering and tactical completeness

Candidate generation reduces the set of considered moves by selecting empty cells near existing stones. This can reduce branching but changes the search problem. The reference cap_loss.json supplies a concrete risk: in the synthetic win fixture at radius one, 20 uncapped candidates include two immediate winning endpoints (7,2) and (7,7), but a cap of six omits both. At depth one, the uncapped score is 9,999,999 and the capped score is 99,990. This is not an Alpha-Beta error: it is a difference in which moves are admitted before the search. It demonstrates why an ordering or cap policy must be evaluated against tactical membership, and why a value equality proof applies only after the move set is fixed [22].

The 23 October engine uses a different candidate policy, with a soft cap that retains immediate tactical completions. Its record includes twelve tactical-completion retention checks. The reference counterexample and the later retention checks therefore describe different policies. A controlled comparison must keep candidate membership fixed before attributing a change in work to ordering or Alpha-Beta pruning.
5.4.3 Hash, table scope and interrupted search

The reference verification record reports 3,998 forward and 3,998 undo hash checks, plus four terminal hash-axis checks. Its table semantics record reports three bound variants and observed exact, lower and upper entries. These checks concern the inspected corpus and implementation. A native entry size of 12 bytes is recorded, but the underlying hash map is not a fixed 8 MB table; reservation or native object size alone does not establish total memory consumption. The record states that rule configuration and root perspective are not included in the key and mate-ply normalization is absent. Those facts constrain safe reuse [50].

The cache-scope probe makes the constraint tangible. For a clustered fixture at radius one and cap eight, a warm table at the same root returns the same score of 0 as the initial search, with nine nodes and eight hits in the probe. After a move changes the root context, the recorded cold score is 0 and the warm score is 19,800. The record characterizes cross-root reuse of root-relative entries as unsupported. A conservative implementation must start with a fresh table or identify all evaluation and rule context in its namespace; the example does not prove that every warm reuse is unsafe [27].

The budget artifact tests restoration during interruption. A direct budget of ten is exhausted and restores the root. In the iterative case, a budget of fifty is exhausted after a completed depth of two; 40 aggregate nodes are reported, and the record explicitly says that aggregate excludes the aborted iteration. It is therefore incorrect to describe 40 as the complete work consumed by all attempted iterations. The last completed result remains meaningful only when incomplete iteration state is not presented as a completed deeper result [51].

5.7 Threats to validity and interpretation

Internal validity. Search comparisons require the same position, depth, terminal rules, evaluation perspective and candidate set. Otherwise an apparent improvement can arise from searching a different tree. A table that ignores rule or perspective context can return a stale value. An aborted iteration must be counted separately from completed work. These issues are directly motivated by the cap-loss, cache-scope and budget probes.

Measurement validity. The native experiments distinguish recursive nodes, leaf evaluations, ranking evaluations, cutoffs and time. Treating one counter as a substitute for all computation can reverse the apparent conclusion, as the clustered ordered example shows. Three sequential timing repeats and lack of randomized order, CPU isolation or uncertainty intervals support descriptive comparisons only. Native timer scope, Worker hydration and search, and browser round-trip duration are different quantities.

External validity. The fixtures cover controlled and seeded boards but not the full space of legal games. Tactical test positions may be synthetic. A 100-game Rule-Based versus Random result is narrow, and it does not calibrate six difficulty levels against human skill. Node execution and headless-browser synthetic input do not establish physical touchscreen, Wink host, deployment or production behavior.

Reproducibility and provenance. The repository supplies raw measurements, harnesses, source excerpts and binary hashes. The 12 November follow-up matched 36 available engine, reference, harness and lock files to their archived hashes and reproduced the non-timing search results. On 13 November, the modified engine was included in the local application source package and rebuilt to the same WebAssembly bytes. The native reference library remains a separately identified dependency. Appendix B records these checks without replacing the dates or environments of the historical experiments.
CHAPTER 6. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
6.1 Work completed and contribution

The project implements a Caro web application and a teaching website for board representation, Freestyle rules, heuristic evaluation and adversarial search. The application connects a React interface and PixiJS board to a Rust/WebAssembly search Worker. The teaching website provides visual explanations and executable Python examples. Weekly reports and native research artifacts document the algorithmic development and its experimental evaluation [1], [53].

The main contribution is an implementation-level account of how game decisions depend on representation and search policy. Board updates, history and rollback support recursive exploration. Terminal utility takes precedence over the static heuristic. Minimax defines alternating decisions, and Alpha-Beta pruning preserves the value of the same selected search tree while omitting branches that cannot change it. Candidate filtering changes the tree itself; ordering changes the sequence in which its moves are examined. The reference experiments extend this analysis to Zobrist hashing, transposition-table bounds and interrupted iterative search [11], [13].

The recorded native engine experiment reports 408 Minimax/Alpha-Beta comparisons with matching values and 820 successful restoration checks. Separate adapter and browser records exercise the connection between search and the application. In the reference experiments, move ordering reduced visits on some positions, but its evaluation work could outweigh the time saved. A hard cap discarded immediate wins in one fixture, and cache reuse after a root-player change returned an incorrect score in another. These results show that depth and node count alone do not assess correctness or efficiency [19], [22], [27], [31], [32], [49].

The final local application provides all six report profiles: Easy, Normal, Hard, Very Hard, Expert and Master. A fresh build from the included Rust source reproduced the existing application binary byte-for-byte. Browser smoke checks selected each profile and observed a response with completed depths 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 on the checked opening. The presentation now embeds this local application. These checks establish the tested configuration and interaction; playing-strength calibration remains future work.
6.2 Limitations

The active search is selective. Its soft tactical cap retains immediate winning and blocking completions, but deeper positional moves remain subject to the candidate limit. The configured limit falls from 15 at Hard to 8 at Master as depth rises from two to five plies. The static evaluator scores contiguous runs; gapped formations and intersecting threats depend on tactical assessment and deeper search. Persistent transposition tables and iterative-deepening budgets are studied in separate implementations rather than used by the active Rust search [10], [13], [29].

The implementation review also identifies boundary cases for further correction. GameController starts a round before validating the first direct move request, and the core coordinate predicate checks bounds without requiring integer indices. The normal pointer path supplies integer cells, while Worker responses have a separate integer check. Drag detection compares consecutive pointer positions, which can miss a slow drag made of small steps. In the teaching website, a failed or missing Pyodide loader can leave initialization state or waiting callers unresolved [2], [35], [37], [43].

The measurements cover a finite corpus and specific native or browser environments. The published Git revision includes the application and binary but omits the complete modified engine and caro-core-reference dependency. The local release now supplies the modified engine and a reproducible application build; reproducing the separate reference experiments still requires their dependency sources. Historical timing and bot-match summaries retain narrower provenance than the controlled research records. Physical-device interaction, live host integration, human usability and calibrated playing strength remain subjects for further evaluation [1], [11], [13], [24], [46], [52].
6.3 Future development

Release maintenance should preserve the source-to-binary connection established by the local rebuild. The modified engine, lockfile, build command and generated-package hashes should be published together. The separate reference library and experiment harnesses should also be distributed with their exact dependencies. Each new experiment should identify its source revision, toolchain, platform and binary hash, while the earlier baseline remains available under its own identity.

Input validation and lifecycle handling should be strengthened at their owning boundaries. The core should require integer coordinates and validate a move before advancing the match phase. Gesture classification should use displacement from the initial press, and the Pyodide loader should settle all waiting requests and permit retry after failure. Regression cases should include invalid first moves, fractional inputs, slow drags and failed runtime initialization.

Further search evaluation should separate candidate selection from move ordering. A fixed corpus of reachable positions can compare all-legal search with radius and cap policies, including known wins, blocks and intersecting threats. Useful outputs include missed tactics, chosen moves, root values, ranking evaluations, recursive visits and elapsed time. Multiple seeds and explicit tie handling would make the comparison less dependent on one fixture.

Persistent caching requires a defined compatibility context. Future work should include rules, evaluation weights, root perspective and mate-distance treatment in the cache design, then test exact, lower and upper bounds across depths and search windows. Warm-table and cold-table comparisons should include root changes and collisions. Memory measurements should include map capacity and allocation overhead as well as entry size.

An anytime search could combine iterative deepening with cancellation and an explicit last-completed-result policy. Its telemetry should distinguish requested depth from completed depth and count work spent in aborted iterations. Tests should cover Reset, Undo, stale replies and Worker failure while confirming that interrupted search restores the input position.

Application evaluation should extend to physical target devices and the intended host environment. Repeated measurements of response latency and frame timing would complement the present automated checks. A participant study could examine control usability and perceived difficulty, while a multi-seed tournament against stated opponents could assess playing strength. Both require a documented protocol before their results can support conclusions.

The teaching website should remain synchronized with the implementations it explains. Illustrative programs need explicit scope, especially where a horizontal example accompanies a four-direction rule description. Charts should link to the data and generation procedure that produced them. This would let readers move from an explanation to the corresponding source or experiment without confusing a demonstration with a measurement.

W07: Candidate neighborhoods, selective search and difficulty configuration.

The first procedure inspects the published revision and runs its frontend scripts. The local release described later in this appendix additionally contains CaroGame/engine and the rebuild script. Its changes are supplied in the local source package; checking out the published SHA alone does not retrieve them. Native research records retain their original harnesses, manifests, results and provenance [1], [11], [13].
git clone https://github.com/tducn110/basicproject.git
cd basicproject
git checkout 7e1e2d51321a4e6b2e26493c34f0a485d4de39cc
git status --short

From the repository root, install the game dependencies from its lockfile, then run the declared typecheck, test and build scripts. Use a Node version compatible with the locked packages and record node --version and npm --version with the results.
cd CaroGame
npm ci
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run build
In a separate terminal at the repository root, install and build the presentation website. The development command starts its interactive preview.
cd present
npm ci
npm run build
npm run dev
To inspect the native experiment provenance from the repository root, read the manifests and recorded results below. These commands do not regenerate the datasets.
cat research/week_05_09/Cargo.toml research/week_05_09/results/provenance.json
cat research/current_2026_10_23/provenance.json
git ls-tree -d --name-only HEAD

The original reference runner requires caro-core-reference at the repository root. The current-engine research runner expects gomoku-main/engine and an application directory named 10_caro; its WASM stage copies generated files into that application. These paths belong to the original experiment workspace. The local application release instead owns its Rust source at CaroGame/engine and uses the following commands from CaroGame to rebuild it. Rust with the wasm32-unknown-unknown target and wasm-pack must be installed; the offline build also requires the locked Cargo dependencies in the local cache.
npm run build:wasm
cargo test --manifest-path engine/Cargo.toml --locked --offline
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run build

The build writes src/game/wasm/engine/provenance.json with the input hashes, output hashes and tool versions. The 13 November build used rustc/cargo 1.98.1 and wasm-pack 0.15.0. The current engine toolchain selects stable, so a later build must record the resolved version and compare its generated hashes rather than assume identical bytes.

For the local defense demonstration, start the game with npm run dev from CaroGame, then start npm run dev from present in another terminal. The game uses port 8443 and the presentation uses port 5174. Local presentation entry points use the game on the same host at port 8443; VITE_CARO_GAME_URL can explicitly select another application endpoint. Open http://localhost:5174 for the presentation or http://localhost:8443 for the game.
